title: CUT&ID for simultaneous profiling of protein-DNA and protein-protein interactions.
data_url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress/studies/E-MTAB-16382 (sequencing + bigwig tracks); https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD071610 (mass spectrometry); supplementary tables 1-4 attached to the paper

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the 22 MB supplement and opened all four Excel tables with openpyxl. Supplementary Table 1 holds eight peak sheets in narrowPeak format (genome coordinates plus peak score, fold-enrichment and two significance columns) with no header row: CTCF 34,941 rows, TCF7L2 24,273, SMARCA4 18,948, H3K27ac 17,445, HDAC1 11,466, RAD21 6,133, beta-catenin 6,282, JUN 4,239 (123,727 peaks total). Supplementary Table 2 lists only the significant proximal proteins per target (33-891 rows each, 5 columns: gene name, significant yes/no, log2 fold change versus an IgG antibody control, p-value, adjusted p-value). Supplementary Table 3 holds the raw protein-group matrix (1,617 proteins x 122 columns for the 8 targets; 3,220 x 50 for the fresh/frozen/fixed comparison), with UniProt accessions present. Supplementary Table 4 holds the merged statistics (2,994 x 239) and a sample sheet showing 4 runs per target (2 biological x 2 technical). I also queried the ArrayExpress study record: 25 bigwig signal tracks, 23.9-91.5 MB each, 1,514 MB total, plus raw reads in ENA (ERP186498), and the PRIDE project record (raw mass spectrometry only).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Antibody identities, the FrIP (fraction of reads in peaks) signal-to-noise values, the 71% overlap with ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq, motif enrichment results, and the claim that fixed/frozen nuclei recover >50% of fresh-sample consensus peaks. I did not download any bigwig track (each exceeds the 50 MB per-file cap) or any raw sequencing or mass-spectrometry file.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplement zip opened locally; ArrayExpress study is public (isPublic true) and PRIDE project is released. No login or access application.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the natural task (predict from DNA sequence where each regulator binds), only positive peak calls are provided; unbound regions do not exist as rows, so the bound/not-bound label must be constructed by sampling background. The only evidence about unbound DNA sits in 25 bigwig signal tracks of 24-92 MB each, over the download cap. The proteomics label 'significant yes/no' is a real column, but Supplementary Table 2 lists only the significant proteins, so negatives again have to be assembled from Table 3/4.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in the files: peaks carry hg38 coordinates (DNA sequence needs one reference genome download, not per-row lookups) and the proteomics tables carry UniProt accessions, so protein sequences are one bulk fetch away.

a4_units_stated.note: Proteomics columns are labelled with units implied by name (log2 fold change, p-value, adjusted p-value) and the Info sheet states the significance cut-off. Peak sheets have no header row at all, but the Info sheet says narrowPeak format, so the columns are interpretable by convention.

a5_enough_rows.note: Row counts look large (123,727 peaks; 1,617 proteins x 8 targets) but the unit that any model would have to generalise over is the target protein, and there are exactly 8 of them, all in one cell line (HCT116), from one lab, with 2 biological replicates each. Leave-one-target-out cross-validation over 8 groups cannot support a model, and the peaks within a target are not independent examples of 'a new regulator'.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~25 MB of Excel tables; +1.5 GB if all bigwig tracks were fetched; +~1 GB for the hg38 reference genome
a6_fits_laptop.note: The tables are trivially small. The signal tracks are individually over the 50 MB cap, so I recorded their names and sizes only.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Verified exactly: the paper's stated 34,941 CTCF peaks, 18,948 SMARCA4, 17,445 H3K27ac, 24,273 TCF7L2, 4,239 JUN, 6,133 RAD21, 11,466 HDAC1 and the protein counts 202/301/36/890/614 all match the sheet row counts.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels trace to physical measurements: peaks are MACS2 statistical calls on sequencing read counts against an IgG antibody control, and protein enrichment is a limma-style test on mass-spectrometry intensities. Not another machine-learning model's output. Caveat: enrichment values partly rest on imputed intensities where a protein was undetected in the control, which the paper states.

part_a_killers.a9_note: A2 and A5 both fail; per the checklist I stopped and did not score Parts B-J.

existing_models.name: ChromBPNet (Kundaje lab), a base-resolution convolutional network that predicts chromatin accessibility and transcription factor footprints from DNA sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved paper and GitHub repository; its authors report it is competitive with much larger models at predicting variant effects, pioneer transcription factor binding and reporter activity across assays and cell contexts, and that it outperformed Enformer on those benchmarks. I did not verify a specific number on a held-out chromosome split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Assay-specific enzyme bias: the model needs an explicit bias-correction step because the cutting enzyme leaves sequence preferences that otherwise get learned as biology.

existing_models.name: deepTFBS, a multi-task and transfer-learning DNA language model for transcription factor binding site prediction
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved 2025 open-access paper; reports improved within- and cross-species prediction, with emphasis on small-sample training. Specific split numbers not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Prediction for transcription factors with few training examples and across species.

existing_models.name: A DNABERT-based deep learning framework for transcription factor binding site prediction (Scientific Reports)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved paper; combines a pretrained DNA language model with convolution and attention. Numbers not verified.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Capturing long-range dependencies alongside local motif features.

existing_models.name: Benchmark of transcription factor binding site prediction models (Briefings in Bioinformatics 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved paper; evaluated position-weight-matrix methods, LS-GKM support vector machines and attention-based deep models on ENCODE optimal IDR-thresholded ChIP-seq peaks for 59 transcription factors.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Which model class wins depends strongly on the transcription factor's DNA-binding domain family.

backbone.name: DNABERT-2 / Nucleotide Transformer for the peak sequences; ESM-2 for the proteomics partners
backbone.hardware: CPU laptop for frozen embeddings of ~124k 200-500 bp peak sequences or ~1,600 proteins
backbone.licence: Backbones permissive; the paper's supplement carries the article's open-access licence (NAR is fully open access).

integration.partner_dataset: ENCODE ChIP-seq for HCT116 (CTCF, RAD21, SMARCA4, H3K27ac, JUN, HDAC1 and more) and BioGRID/IntAct for protein-protein interactions
integration.join_key: hg38 genomic coordinates for the peaks; UniProt accession / gene symbol for the proteins
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a sequence model trained on ENCODE ChIP-seq transfer to peaks called by a different assay chemistry (antibody-tethered nuclease plus proximity biotinylation) — a real transfer question, but one answerable on 8 targets only as an anecdote, and the paper already answers the descriptive version by reporting 71% peak overlap for CTCF.

controls.positive_control: CTCF motif must be the top enriched motif in CTCF and RAD21 peaks (the paper reports exactly this), and cohesin subunits must rank top among CTCF proximal proteins.
controls.negative_control: The IgG isotype-control samples (bigwig tracks and proteomics columns) are genuine experimental negatives, plus label shuffling.
controls.external_validation: ENCODE HCT116 ChIP-seq for the same factors; BioGRID/IntAct for known interactors.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built on this supplement could only claim: for eight chromatin regulators profiled in one colorectal cancer cell line by one lab, DNA sequence predicts which of the regions this assay called as peaks are the strongest — a claim that says nothing about a ninth regulator or a second cell type.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use DNA sequence and protein sequence to predict where chromatin regulators bind and which proteins sit next to them
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered: 123,727 peak regions across 8 chromatin regulators (verified row counts) as DNA sequence windows, and 1,617 mass-spectrometry-detected proteins paired with each of the same 8 regulators as protein sequences.
plain_idea.predict: Either peak strength (fold-enrichment over an antibody control, a column in the peak table) from DNA sequence, or whether a protein is an enriched neighbour of a given regulator (a log2 fold-change column from mass spectrometry of streptavidin-captured biotinylated proteins).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Nobody has modelled paired DNA-binding and protein-neighbour data measured in the same sample, so the combination is genuinely new; but with eight regulators in one cell line there is no way to show a model generalises to a regulator it has not seen.

more_or_better_data.why: ENCODE already provides ChIP-seq in HCT116 for most of these eight factors, and the paper benchmarks against it (71% of CUT&ID CTCF peaks shared with ENCODE ChIP-seq). Eight targets from one lab is far less data than the 59-plus factor ENCODE sets the existing models train on.

confidence_score.why: Two biological replicates per genomics target and four mass-spectrometry runs per proteomics target allow a replicate-based noise estimate, but peaks were called on merged replicates, so per-peak reproducibility is not directly in the supplied tables.

models_beatable.why: ChromBPNet (2024-2025, bias-corrected base-resolution convolutional network, open code and weights) and the 2025 Briefings in Bioinformatics benchmark are recent, open and honestly evaluated on held-out ENCODE data; nothing here gives an edge over them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The condition that fails is 'our model sees everything the baseline sees plus new data': this assay measures the same quantity with a different chemistry on far fewer targets, so adding it to an ENCODE-trained model adds assay variation rather than information.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: (a) predict transcription factor and histone-mark binding, or peak strength, from hg38 sequence using a frozen DNA language model with a small head, trained on the 123,727 CUT&ID peaks; (b) predict which of 1,617 detected proteins is an enriched proximal partner of a given regulator from paired protein-sequence embeddings. (a) needs constructed negatives and competes directly with open, well-evaluated models trained on far more ENCODE data; (b) has only 8 bait proteins, so a leave-one-bait-out evaluation would mostly measure which proteins are non-specifically sticky.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the Excel tables parsed in seconds on this laptop; the embedding figure assumes ~124,000 peak sequences through a small DNA language model on CPU at a few sequences per second, and the working set is dominated by the hg38 reference genome, not by the supplement.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the independent units rather than the rows: 8 target proteins, 1 cell line, 2 biological replicates. That number is visible in Supplementary Table 4's sample sheet in under a minute and kills both project framings.

verdict_reason: A methods paper with clean, count-matching supplementary tables, but the generalisation unit is 8 chromatin regulators in one cell line from one lab (A5 fails), and the DNA-binding label is positives-only so bound-versus-unbound would have to be constructed (A2 fails); the sequence-to-binding task is also already served by open, honestly evaluated models trained on much larger ENCODE data.
